Cattle Rustling

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR MORE STRINGENT LEGISLATION AND GOVERNMENT ACTION TO DETER CATTLE RUSTLING
speechtext:
That this House, recognizing that cattle rustling is now a big-time criminal racket aided by modern methods and encouraged by high profits and low risk, and has become a serious problem to western cattlemen and the cattle industry, urges the government to enact deterrent cattle rustling laws and to mount an RCMP enforcement offensive against such criminal racketeers.
He said: At the outset, Mr. Speaker, may I say I am pleased that this subject, a favourite of mine since it deals with the cattle industry, is before us for discussion during the private members' hour. Let me begin by briefly recounting the history, the background of cattle rustling in Canada. "Theft" would, of course, be another way of describing it, but cattle rustling is a term which has been glorified, in a way, over the years.
There is nothing new about cattle rustling in western Canada where its incidence is traditionally much higher than in the eastern regions of Canada. As I say, there is much folklore relating to this subject. There are many stories, for example, of cattle herds becoming established as a result of a fast horse and a long and sure loop. There are other stories of unbranded calves being tied by the neck to another calf and trained to follow a new mother cow, resulting in a supposedly very prolific cow herd, with a strong tendency for twins! The owners of such herds were usually considered to be top hands with a rope.
In the early days before fencing, when great cattle herds were the rule, branding was often delayed until mid-summer giving ample time for the unauthorized branding of apparent strays or for the altering of existing brands by means of a quickly heated "running" iron-usually a wagon endgate iron rod with a round eye that could be used to make any combination of brands. Considerable folklore is attached to these stories but there is also concrete evidence that rustling along these lines-and in other ways-did indeed take place. One dramatic piece of western cattle rustling folklore that I have been unable to obtain positive proof of is the stringing-up of the cattle thief on the end of a rope, hung from a convenient limb of a cottonwood tree, out in the middle of the bald prairie where trees just do not grow.
Be that as it may, theft of cattle in various forms still presents a serious problem to the industry and there are clear indications that cattle rustling is on the increase. Rustling in modern days, at least in western Canada, falls into three categories. The first involves the theft of very young calves, usually less than a week old and still unbranded. Most calves are not branded until they are between two and three months of age. These young calves usually spend most of their first few days lying down in a concealed spot not far from their mothers. It is an easy matter to catch such a calf, on foot, without a horse, and toss it into the trunk of a car. A young calf like this must be immediately transplanted to another cow if it is to live. This is a difficult job but not an impossible one for an experienced stockman. The insidious part of this form of

February 24, 1975
Cattle Rustling
theft is that the thief is usually someone from your own neighbourhood. It is difficult to sell such young calves because most auction markets have regulations for bidding sales of very young calves.
The second category concerns the shooting of cattle, mainly in the fall of the year, usually during the hunting season. When meat prices are high-and they have been high over the last several years-it is a strong temptation for a hunter who has been unsuccessful in a game hunt to shoot a young, grass-fat steer, or heifer, or a cow, dress it out on the spot and put the carcass in a deep freezer at home. Very often such crimes take place near our larger cities and in far too many cases liquor is a factor in the deliberate actions of these unsuccessful game hunters.
The third category of cattle theft is the most daring and deliberate and it is premeditated and planned well in advance. In this type of theft any number of cows, from one or two to complete truckloads, are brazenly stolen for disposal later, usually in another province. In most cases they are trucked many miles, usually to another province-and in one case they were trucked across the United States border; this occurred within the last year-to a distant, live cattle market where they are sold and the covering brand on the stolen cattle is claimed as the legal brand of the thief.
Some provincial brand departments now have computerized brand records, and this is definitely helping to contain this form of rustling. In other cases the stolen cattle are trucked or even trailed on foot to another location where the brands are altered or "worked" into an entirely new brand. A conviction was recently obtained for this kind of theft in southern Alberta, and the thief was caught because he did not allow the altered brand time enough to heal properly with a new hair coat before he tried to sell the cattle. In this particular case a considerable number of cattle were involved; he got a little overconfident.
In still further cases these animals are privately butchered and the meat sold privately, or goes into the deep freeze again. These kinds of thefts can occur anywhere in Canada where cattle are confined for feeding. Just recently there was a case of some six to ten head reported stolen from a farm not far from Ottawa. These cattle were out of a herd of about 300 head, and the thefts took place over a one-month period.
I should now like to comment on the specifics of cattle rustling, convictions, and sentences passed on these cattle thieves. In earlier days punishment on conviction was much more severe than it is today. Today a person convicted of rustling or theft of cattle usually receives a sentence of one day in jail and a fine, or a suspended sentence, or jail from one day to six months. Very seldom does a convicted rustler receive a sentence of over six months unless he had previous convictions of some note.
Cattle theft charges are usually brought under section 294 of the Criminal Code. If the value of the property, in this case cattle, is over $200, the penalty can go as high as ten years' imprisonment. In other words, the traditional sentences passed on modern-day cattle thieves are com-

pletely unrealistic, as in most cases all mature animals stolen are worth well over $200.
Under section 400 of the Criminal Code, sentences for killing, maiming, wounding, poisoning or injuring cattle allow up to five years in jail. In comparison, breaking and entering under section 306 calls for a penalty of up to life imprisonment if the premises broken into are a dwelling-house, and up to 14 years if the place is other than a dwelling-house. Most breaking and entering convictions involve far less value than the value of cattle stolen or killed.
I suggest that consideration should also be given to the small cattle producer who raises only a few head, or feeds a few head, for whom cattle theft represents a loss of a large part of his profit considering the size of his operation. I must say that it must be most discouraging to law officers, provincial brand offices and cattle producers when the penalty imposed is very light or the case is dismissed. In some cases, such as in the area of the foothills country west of Calgary, cattlemen have organized viligante groups to patrol their own areas at night, especially during the hunting season. The purpose is, of course, to protect their own property and cattle.
In only one case that I am aware of has there been a more realistic sentence for cattle theft, and this was very recently. It was a case that occurred north of Edmonton and a sentence of two years was given for butchering a cow on an Indian reserve. The accomplice in this particular case was sentenced to nine months. Both were charged under section 294 of the Criminal Code for theft of property over $200.
In Alberta over the last five complete years-that is, from 1970 through to 1974 inclusive-there were 10,859 cattle reported missing, another 1,248 reported stolen; 196 cattle were recovered and 161 convictions were obtained. This figure for convictions applies only to the first four years, not to the year 1974; I presume they were not available for that year. During 1974, the final year within the bracket, in Alberta some 225 cases showed some evidence of cattle offences, as a result of which 45 charges were laid by police. I have been unable to obtain the number of convictions in Alberta in 1974.
Over the same five year period-1970 to 1974 inclusive- in Saskatchewan some 5,457 head were reported missing, of which 1,479 were recovered. These Saskatchewan figures are higher-that is to say, the incidence of theft is on the increase-in spite of increased surveillance by farmers, provincial stock inspectors and the RCMP. In 1974, in Saskatchewan, only three persons were charged with theft of cattle; two of these were convicted and the third case is still outstanding. I have been unable to obtain the number of charges laid in Saskatchewan during 1974; I presume there were a fair number.
In British Columbia, the B.C. Cattlemen's Association have assured me that the incidence of cattle rustling is still probably on the increase and they want to see heavier sentences on conviction. They suggest that if longer jail sentences are not appropriate for the courts-and sometimes we seem to think that is the only reason for not giving longer jail sentences-then the B.C. Cattlemen's Association would like to see much heavier fines handed
February 24, 1975

out as a meaningful deterrent, and in this respect I certainly agree with them.
I want to read a resolution that was passed at the last annual meeting of the Western Stock Growers Association, which is the Alberta commercial cattlemen's group that met in Edmonton earlier this month. One resolution that is right on this subject reads as follows:
Whereas it is our understanding that special livestock investigators of K Division, RCMP are unable to advance in rank beyond corporal while remaining on this assignment,
And whereas this encourages good experienced men to accept transfer to other assignments at about the time that their accumulated experience could be most useful to the lifestock industry
Therefore be it resolved that we continue to request the formation of a separate branch within the RCMP for livestock investigators.
They pointed out during the discussion of this resolution that lack of advancement for special stock investigators is a real factor in getting good, qualified RCMP officers to specialize in this type of work.
In drawing my remarks to a close, I wish to suggest very seriously that there is a twofold need in our Canadian cattle industry to reduce cattle theft and other unaccounted for losses that cannot be documented. First of all, I suggest there is a genuine need for much stiffer penalties, either jail sentences or fines, or both, by our courts of law. Secondly, we need stepped up surveillance and inspection by the RCMP with the formation of a separate branch within the RCMP for this purpose.
If it would be in order, Mr. Speaker, I should like to suggest that I would be willing to withdraw my notice of motion to allow this subject matter to be referred to the Standing Committee on Agriculture for further decision and referral for action to the two departments concerned, the Department of Justice and the office of the Solicitor General. I would truly hope there is enough broad interest on all sides of the House that this subject will be allowed to go to the committee this afternoon.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR MORE STRINGENT LEGISLATION AND GOVERNMENT ACTION TO DETER CATTLE RUSTLING
speechtext:
I am not going to take up too much time during this debate, as the hon. member for Medicine Hat has very adequately and eloquently put the position of Canadian cattlemen with regard to cattle rustling. There is a lot of concern about cattle rustling in the provinces where cattle raising is practised. I have received a number of representations from cattlemen in British Columbia, particularly after my introduction of a private member's bill at the session
Cattle Rustling
before this and at this session. I have received a number of calls from all over the prairie region in respect of that bill, most of which were in favour of seeing the contents adopted.
My particular bill would stiffen the penalties for cattle rustling. This has been one of the greatest concerns of cattlemen, that the penalties being dished out have not been stiff enough to act as a deterrent to future cattle rustlers. My bill would have done the following:
Every person who commits theft of cattle is guilty of an indictable offence and is liable
(a)	to imprisonment for ten years, where the value of the cattle
exceed fifty dollars, or
(b)	to imprisonment for two years, where the value of the cattle does
not exceed fifty dollars provided that a minimum sentence in either
case shall be imprisonment for one year.
I am not going to be dogmatic about this as I know the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang) and the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) are giving this consideration. Private member's bills do not always see the light of day, but I suggest the purpose of bringing these bills forward-and I suspect this is the purpose of the hon. member's motion-is to make sure that the government of Canada realizes that the cattlemen in this country are concerned about this serious problem of cattle rustling. It is still a problem in this country. I have a copy of a press release by the British Columbia Cattlemen which points out that ranchers in that province each year lose between 200 and 400 head to cattle rustlers. This is still a very serious problem and I would concur in the words of the hon. member for Medicine Hat in respect of this problem.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR MORE STRINGENT LEGISLATION AND GOVERNMENT ACTION TO DETER CATTLE RUSTLING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, coming from an area where cattle rustling is a very recent thing, I am pleased to support this motion. I am also pleased that the parliamentary secretary has indicated there is little disagreement with the suggestion that it be referred to the committee. I would like to see that action taken, but I would offer a word of caution in respect of the use of the RCMP in a special way under this legislation, particularly in Ontario and Quebec where we have provincial police forces which enforce the Criminal Code. It would be rather difficult for the RCMP to get involved in an investigation that normally takes place under the jurisdiction of the provincial police force.
Cattle rustling is a very insidious type of theft, the type that does lend itself to vigilante action. I think this is an additional reason for providing strong enough penalties to discourage this type of theft. I know of the case of a farmer who left his farm under the care of his 15 year-old son. The son heard a truck back up to the barn door. He got a gun and went out to see what was happening. When the driver of the truck had finished loading cattle, he advanced toward the son, who shot and killed him. It was finally decided that the son shot in self-defence because the man advanced toward him; therefore, the boy was being attacked. I would suggest that this is not the way to solve the problem. We must come up with a better solution. If this motion should become a legislative act of this parliament, we should include in it some way of forcing insurance companies to live up to their insurance bargains.

Cattle Rustling
I live in an area where we have a federal community pasture. The cattle put into that pasture are insured against loss. The government does not supply continuous supervision of the pasture and each year four or five head of cattle are lost. When the farmer learns of the theft, which is usually when he takes the cattle out of the pasture or when the supervisor informs the farmers collectively that according to his count there are not enough cattle in the pasture, he reports it to the insurance company and makes a claim. However, in no case of which I am aware has the insurance company been willing to accept its responsibility. They decline to pay on two grounds. First, they say that the claim was made too long after the fact for there to be any effective police action and therefore the company has not been notified by the farmer within a reasonable time or in time for the police to carry out an investigation. For that reason they renounce their responsibility and refuse to make payment.
The second ground on which the insurance companies refuse to make payment is that the farmer cannot prove that the animal he put into the community pasture is the animal that was stolen from it, or that he no longer has possession of the animal. In other words, the suggestion is that he may have taken it home, and the company refuses to pay.
As a result, it seems to me that we are faced with a problem in that the farmer is not able to defend his own property, particularly in the way the young lad did to whom I referred. I suggest that we are not prepared to allow farmers to protect their property in that way. In addition, I am not in favour of establishing in Ontario vigilante groups of farmers to protect their cattle either during the hunting season or during the off-season. If we are not willing to allow that, then we must assure the farmers that somebody else will do it.
I think our police forces should have the assurance that, if they do the work that is necessary leading to a conviction, that conviction will be a deterrent to others. It is quite easy, regardless of whether it is in western or eastern Canada, for a person to drive by a field with some cattle in it and to take one animal without any difficulty. In most instances cattle are domesticated and not hard to catch. The rustler can put the cattle in this truck, be on his way, and later slaughter the cattle for his own use or for limited commercial use. The reward is considerable and the risk fairly small.
Protection must be given in a number of ways. We should develop a system of marking cattle that is more effective than the one we use now, namely, the system of ear tags. As soon as the ear tag is removed, the evidence is gone. It is. quite true that a farmer, if he has only 200 or 300 head of cattle, can tell whether one is his cow or not. But it is difficult to prove in court. It can be proven by the hide, but in any case it is difficult.
Farmers must be protected by law, from this type of theft, and I agree with the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Hargrave) that the penalties for this type of theft must be increased. The difficulty that I see with this motion-and of course the committee would be able to deal with the problem-is with regard to jurisdiction. As

I said, in Ontario and Quebec different police methods are used from those in western Canada, and therefore the act as it affects Quebec and Ontario would be limited in scope unless a change where made in the administration of the RCMP. Since I do not think such a change is likely to take place, I think the act will have to be amended to include other police forces in those areas.
The other point is with regard to the valuation of the animals. The hon. member for Kamloops-Cariboo (Mr. Marchand) mentioned a minimum of $50. Perhaps this might be effective now, but it would certainly not have been effective in the case of a dropped calf a day or two old, a year or year and half ago. So if we accept the minimum of $50, the animals that are being stolen would not even be worth carrying away. Cattle should be valued fairly highly. It is hard to tell what the figure should be when you are dealing with a carcass, even if the carcass is available, which in most cases it is not.
My main concern is that one of the ways in which the farmer has tried to protect himself has been through insurance. The second way has been to have his animal graze on a community pasture where there is some supervision. In my area a number of farmers have been disappointed in both respects. They have not been able to collect insurance on the animals they have had in the community pasture, and the insurance companies have held the federal government responsible for negligence in supervision. The companies have argued and debated the point successfully as to whether or not a farmer can prove that the animal he put in such a pasture is no longer there. Although they agree that the total count has been reduced, they are not willing to accept that a particular animal has disappeared, because of the difficulty in proving when it disappeared.
I hope that the notice of motion put forward by the hon. member will receive the approval of the House and will, in time, become legislation because, in view of the high cost of meat today and the inability to supervise pastures or even stables, there has been a great increase in rustling in Ontario as well as in western Canada. If we allow the legislation to remain as it is now, farmers will be inclined and strongly motivated to defend their own property in their own way. If we allow this, those who condemn the use of fire arms, will find an increase in their use because farmers will be forced to defend their own property. Accidental shootings will occur when farmers decide to defent themselves against a fairly organized group of people engaged in rustling.
There are indications in my area that many of the thefts that are taking place are well planned and well thought out. Some organization moves in from another community and a number of thefts take place in one night. There was a case in the Toronto stockyards this year of the provincial police being able to give a description of the truck used by rustlers. The truck was stopped in the stockyard, the owners of the truck were apprehended and the cattle returned to the area. But that was an exceptional case.
Most of the thefts are successful, and for that reason farmers are overly apprehensive about the thefts that take place, about the inability of the police to do anything and the willingness of insurance companies to compensate for the thefts. Farmers are in a mood to take matters in their
February 24, 1975

own hands, so I strongly urge the committee to consider seriously accepting the motion before us today.

speakeroldname: Mr. Gilles Marceau (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR MORE STRINGENT LEGISLATION AND GOVERNMENT ACTION TO DETER CATTLE RUSTLING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I enter this debate not because I believe I am an expert on farm or animal matters, far from that, but to indicate on behalf of the department I am representing the legal aspect of the matter now before us.
But let me first commend the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Hargrave) for the truly honest and interesting way in which he explained the problem, a very serious one as may easily be concluded.
Statistical data submitted by the hon. member clearly show the problem has reached alarming proportions, so it seems quite normal for the government to consider the question and look for a possible solution in a relatively near future.
Sections 283 and 294 as well as paragraph 298(3) of the Criminal Code apply. Section 283 gives a definition of a theft.
Under section 294, where the value of what is stolen does not exceed $200 the penalty is imprisonment for up to two years. Where the value of what is stolen exceeds $200, the person who committed the theft is liable to imprisonment for a maximum ten years. Paragraph 298(3) provides that where an accused is charged with theft of cattle, the burden of proving that the cattle came lawfully in the possession of the accused rests with the latter.
In addition to sections applicable to theft of cattle, paragraph 298(3) of the Criminal Code states the act of fraudulently taking cattle that are found astray or fraudulently defacing a brand or mark on cattle is an indictable offence. Such offences entail imprisonment for five years.
Cattle industry representatives, in their briefs, suggest sentences imposed for theft of cattle do not have the adequate preventive effect needed in this type of criminal act. The hon. member also made representations to that effect. The representatives of cattle breeders also expressed the opinion that the Criminal Code should impose a minimum penalty on cattle rustling.
At their meeting in May 1973, the attorneys general tried to see whether the Criminal Code might be amended concerning cattle theft. Unfortunately, we could not come to an agreement. While representatives of a province recommended imposing a minimum penalty, spokesmen for other provinces proposed to amend the Criminal Code so that cattle rustling be made a crime liable to ten years' imprisonment.
For some time, there has been a clear tendency in amendments to the code to avoid minimum penalties. It results from the fact that the people in charge of the administration of justice generally believe that courts should be left the freedom to impose the sentence that they feel is the most appropriate in each case. If the attorney general considers the sentence inappropriate, he may appeal.
Fully aware of the problems created by cattle rustling, the government hopes to move a bill to amend the Criminal Code appropriately during this session.
Cattle Rustling
Although it is up to Parliament to enact criminal legislation, enforcing the consequential regulations and the provisions of the Criminal Code rests with the provincial authorities, as my hon. friend knows.
Thus I must say to the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Hargrave) that his problem, as he knows, has already been examined by the government, but the representations he made today may urge them to act more rapidly and, as I think we should do, without any referring to a committee. I believe that this study makes it unnecessary to refer the problem to a committee for the time being, as I hopefully think-and of course this is not a commitment- we may admit among ourselves that it is quite likely this matter will soon result in concrete measures.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR MORE STRINGENT LEGISLATION AND GOVERNMENT ACTION TO DETER CATTLE RUSTLING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to congratulate the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Hargrave) for bringing forward this most worth-while motion concerning cattle rustling, and to note as well the comments by the hon. member for Kamloops-Cariboo (Mr. Marchand), who has a private member's bill on the order paper of similar portent that is, directed toward stiffer fines for cattle rustling and action by the government to provide some deterrent with respect to this very serious problem.
The hon. member outlined the representations he had received from groups in western Canada, the various stock producer groups, and I think that he had it very well documented, but I believe that this problem exists-perhaps not on as broad a scale because the cattle populations may not be as great-in Ontario as well. Of course the policing there is done by the Ontario provincial police.
It seems to me that this motion should be given serious consideration by the government. I know that in my own area, especially during this past year and a half when cattle prices have risen to very high levels-of course they have fallen off somewhat since the peak period-there were many cases of animals being rustled. I refer not only to the classic example of an animal being driven away, or loaded and carried away, but often animals were slaughtered right on the farm and the Carcasses taken away. Sometimes it seemed to be a more wasteful and senseless situation, where the more valuable rear quarters of the animal would be taken away and the remainder left to rot on the ground.
It seems to me, when we look at all the difficulties of farming today and the disparity in prices, that often the most valuable animal, that is, the fat, finished animal, is the one which will be stolen or rustled and slaughtered. It is not just confined to the beef animal. Often in my own constituency of Algoma dairy animals are stolen and slaughtered. Of course in this instance the animals involved are valuable. The farmer is not only losing the animal but also the milk which would be produced over the years.
I am very happy to join with other hon. members who are looking toward stiffer fines and deterrents with respect to this serious problem for our farm population.

Mr. Chairman, in making some comments and asking some questions on clause 4 of Bill C-49 I want to begin by supporting the amendment which has been proposed by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain. It seems to me that the suggestion that certain subclauses of clause 4 and certain subclauses of clause 7 should be held in abeyance until the first ministers' meeting has been held would not only be appropriate but, I think, would be only common courtesy. The Premier of Saskatchewan, Premier A. E. Blakeney, wired the Minister of Finance on February 18 suggesting such a procedure, and I imagine that other premiers would also welcome the government's agreement to this request.
I think it should be kept in mind that almost a year ago now the Prime Minister met with the premiers of the provinces in this city in an effort to resolve a very difficult problem. That problem was that the oil-producing provinces, facing a rapid depletion of their oil and gas resources, wanted higher prices to buttress them against the very serious crises that were facing them for the future, whereas the federal government wanted to keep prices below the world price. I would point out, Mr. Chairman, that we in this party in this House of Commons

supported the government in every possible endeavour to keep the price down, and exercised what little influence we had with some of the provincial governments to keep the price down.
Out of that discussion between the Prime Minister and the premiers of the provinces, the oil-producing provinces agreed to a price of $6.50 a barrel despite the fact that the international price was much higher. The Prime Minister, who was very glad to succeed in getting such a concession, came out of the conference saying this was a great day for Canadian federalism, and he praised the premiers of the two provinces for taking steps which we all, including the government, welcomed.
The premiers of the provinces went back to their respective capitals convinced that an agreement had been reached with respect to the matter of resources and that an agreement had been reached with respect to the revenues they could anticipate getting from their resources. They were hardly home before the Minister of Finance, who must have been privy to those discussions at the first ministers' conference, brought down a budget which changed the whole picture with respect to the revenues which would go to the different levels of government from resource taxation. It is little wonder that the premiers were indignant and hostile-little wonder that they expressed the opinion that they had been double-crossed and that no information had been given to them that the government intended to bring down the kind of provisions which are in this legislation, particularly in clauses 4 and 7.
It seems to me that it would fair and proper that the government should agree not to proclaim these clauses that are so controversial until after the first ministers' meeting. It would do the premiers the courtesy of allowing them to have their day in court to present their case to the Prime Minister and his colleagues. If they can persuade the Prime Minister and his colleagues that the measures contained in Bill C-49 are detrimental to the best interests of this country and are harmful to the international community, then the government does not need to proclaim these controversial clauses.
On the other hand if the government is not convinced, it has lost nothing; it can then, by order in council, proclaim the offensive clauses and they would come into effect. All the government will have done then will have been to show some courtesy to the premiers, having given them an opportunity to express their opinions.
It is rather significant that when the matter was one of deciding how much or how little revenue the provinces would get, there was a conference. Everybody was appealed to on the grounds of national interest. Provinces were asked to take less money than they could otherwise have secured. But when it comes to how much revenue the federal government is going to take in resource taxes, that is done without consultation, without any opportunity for the provinces to sit around the table to develop and present their respective points of view. I can understand why the provinces feel very resentful about this matter.
As has already been said, a precedent was set last year in the government's handling of the foreign investment
February 24, 1975

review bill. I think all opposition parties asked the government not to proclaim Part II until the matter had been further investigated and the provinces had been consulted. The government acceded to that request. It has not proclaimed Part II, and whether that decision is wise or unwise is a matter for debate. At least the government recognized that the provinces have an interest in what is done in this House, particularly in matters which affect their jurisdiction.
For as long as I have watched the Liberal Party at close quarters, that party has held itself out as the champion of national unity. It is the party which "can hold Canada together." Yet some actions the party has taken recently have done more to destroy national unity than anything else that has been done for many years. It is difficult to explain that attitude.
I listened to the Minister of Finance say on a radio interview, that we would not agree to postpone the proclamation of any part of this bill because, after all, the government had been given a majority, it had introduced the May budget, and the people had given their approval. I doubt whether the public was aware of the implication of the clauses we are now discussing. I doubt if this was a public issue. I doubt if even the premiers are fully aware of the implications of clauses 4 and 7. The position of the Minister of Finance that the government, because of its majority, can ride roughshod over the rights of this House and of the provincial governments is a shortsighted one.
This country is in trouble. This government is in trouble; it must deal with unemployment, with inflation, with transportation which in the words of one of its own members is in a mess, and with housing difficulties. It needs the co-operation of provincial governments and it is not doing what it should to secure that co-operation.
Why do I say that? In March, 1974, the government obtained concessions from the provinces. Then, some months afterwards, the government did something which could do nothing but antagonize and hurt the provinces, and discourage the kind of co-operation which is necessary if there is to be unity in this country.
Let me deal briefly with some other matters. First, let me ask the minister; what is the rationale behind refusing corporations the right to deduct, from their income tax payments, royalty payments and taxes paid to provinces? This has never been done in the history of Canada. For years it has been recognized that royalties paid to the Crown in right of a province were to be exempt from income tax. Now, without warning, an unprecedented step has been taken. In the second reading debate the Minister of Finance said that the government is doing this because it has the right to a share of resource revenue. I submit that there are other ways in which the federal government can obtain its share of resource revenue.
I also point out, that the Minister of Finance has overlooked something else. Royalties are not taxes in the ordinary sense of the word, in the sense that they are income that can be repeated over a period of years. The royalties to which this legislation applies, that is, royalties on minerals, oil and gas, are paid on rapidly depleting resources. They are payments which are made to the provinces for the loss of an important part of their public domain which cannot be replaced. It is interesting to note,
Income Tax
and if I am wrong I hope the minister will correct me, that we do not adopt this position with renewable resources. But with respect to non-renewable resources, resources with respect to which the federal government ought not to deprive provincial governments of revenue, the government has adopted its position as outlined in this bill.
The minister has also lost sight of something else. The royalties which a provincial government receives do not represent a net gain. Not only do they represent payment for a depleting resource; they represent also payment for the infrastructure which the provincial government must supply if resources are to be effectively extracted. You cannot put down a mine or set up an oil industry or gas industry without building roads, establishing towns or villages, or without building houses, schools and hospitals. In short, in order to make such industries effective and productive, the province must provide almost the entire infrastructure. So the money which a province receives from royalties is not clear gain, is not "buckshee" as it were. A good part of these revenues must be spent by the province, either to build infrastructure or to provide funds for future exploration and development.
On examining this legislation one gets the uneasy feeling that there is a sinister motive behind it, and that the non-deductibility of royalty payments is merely a step to discouraging provincial governments from moving into the ownership and the control of the oil and gas industry. After some of the provinces said, "We might as well take those industries over for ourselves", the minister, either on radio or television said, "Well, we can tax Crown corporations". If this legislation represents the first step in preventing provincial governments from moving into the ownership and control of resource development, it is very sinister legislation indeed. All over the world, except in north America-Mexico is an exception because that country nationalized its oil industry long ago-governments are moving to take over control of the oil and gas industry.
Despite anything the federal government may do, the provinces may be forced into this field. Actually, the federal government itself is being forced into it. The great oil companies which used to talk about standing on their own feet, not depending on the government, and opposing government intervention, now say, "We shall put up a plant to extract oil from the tar sands, provided you give us $1 billion. We shall build a pipe line from Sarnia to Montreal provided you guarantee us from any loss." So we are getting government intervention already, except that it is intervention on the terms of the oil companies.
