like the Liberals; they did not have a chance and they did not know it.

Mr. Chairman, I think that this suggestion by Falconbridge, of Lac Dufault, is worth its weight in gold. We do not ask the government to delete clause 4, but we ask them to hold meetings with the provincial authorities before coming to a final decision because, as the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas) and the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) said, it is true that there is now some disagreement between the provinces and the federal government. It is so true that, in other areas, Quebec Liberal members in Ottawa are being accused by the premier of Quebec of plotting behind his back to defeat him as leader of the Liberal party in Quebec.
Shame!

Everybody knows that. I saw the premier on television the night before last, I read the newspapers yesterday morning. Is the premier right or not? I do not know, it is none of my business, but the premier goes after the Quebec Liberal members in Ottawa saying that they are the ones who challenge his leadership in the province of Quebec. So the Liberals from Quebec are displeased. Mr. Lougheed of Alberta is displeased. Mr. Schreyer of Manitoba is displeased. Mr. Barrett of British Columbia is displeased. Mr. Davis is not pleased either. That one is never pleased!
Mr. Chairman, if at a new meeting or the next meeting of premiers with the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) that issue were discussed so as to allow for an expansion of our naturel resources it seems to me that would help the whole country. Assistance for Alberta, favourable fallouts for Quebec or the Maritimes, favourable fallouts for western Canada, that is what needs to be examined.

Income Tax
Mr. Chairman, if this bill prevents the creation of new industries and jobs which would promote the development of our resources, could it be that the government is more interested in paying out unemployment insurance benefits, welfare allowances than granting tax exemptions to help private enterprise-I do not say free enterprise, free to exploit and rip off everybody-but an honest private enterprise?
That makes a difference.

That makes a
difference.
Government or private enterprise; there is a difference between the two and they don't know it.
You have to find a lamp to find it.

All right, you help me and we will find it.

Mr. Chairman, I think instead of contributing social welfare allowances, we should do like the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) and say: From now on, we assure you that you will get a $5,000 guaranteed annual income. If you earn $4,000 a year, you will be paid $1,000, and if you earn $5,025 a year, you will be paid nothing.
Instead of contributing social welfare allowances and unemployment insurance benefits, the government should grant tax exemptions which would enable private companies to create new jobs and expand their industries. If the creation of 15 new mining sites were made possible in my area, there would not be one unemployed worker left; we now have a 14 per cent rate of unemployment instead. The companies that might develop a copper, zinc, silver, nickel or gold mining prospect do not want to move their little finger because they think the government will snatch everything away. That is an important matter which the Department of Finance should look into. The minister with his top advisers, the government in cabinet should study the possibility of actually helping fight not only unemployment, but inflation too.
Mr. Chairman, a good fifteen new mining companies would suddenly spring into existence in my area. But we keep getting the same shilly-shallying, the same procrastination, and the government, as soon as there is some talk about establishing such a new company, comes up with its threats: "We are going to increase your taxes, to tax your royalties, to tax subsidies, we are going to crush you down." That is what provinces are fighting against now.
Those were the few comments I wanted to make. I would like the Minister of Finance to take into consideration the suggestion I got from Mr. Wright, the Manager of Dufault Lake Falconbridge Copper Limited Company. He made that suggestion, but other corporations might have as well. The mining industry is worried. They are waiting for the government and the Minister of Finance to assure them that they will be able to operate their mines with a profit, instead of at a loss.

And profits in the mining industry are not so exorbitant either. The price of copper is down. In the case of gold, nobody knows. Its price on the world or so-called open market is quite high, but it is still in a tight or restrained situation on the official or legal market.
Mr. Chairman, if the minister contemplates the possible creation of new mining industries, let him wait until he has had discussions again with the provinces, especially if the meeting is to take place on April 15 at the latest. This question should be settled once and for all, so that each and every province may be assured that its autonomy will be respected. They need the assurance that the federal government will help them and provide them with the necessary means for their full development. Then the Minister of Finance will have been of great service not only to provincial governments, but to the whole Canadian population as well.

Mr. Chairman, I rise to support the amendment moved by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain as I believe that clauses 4 and 7 should not be proclaimed until after the first ministers' meeting. I think that when the minister spoke to the Canadian Club in Toronto he had this in mind. He was speaking of the economy, and when he came to the oil and gas industry he said that the third problem involved providing incentives for the development of new energy reserves without permitting oil and gas prices to rise more quickly than is appropriate or necessary.
The minister stated, as reported in the Globe and Mail of January 28:
We have long recognized the need to narrow the differential between the domestic and international price of petroleum to encourage both the development of new reserves and the conservation of existing stocks.
The minister also suggested at that time that the timing and extent of increases in domestic oil prices would be a foremost concern at the federal-provincial meetings in April. He said that within a reasonable period the major elements of uncertainty in the resource field, including taxation, pricing and markets, should be resolved.
Keeping this in mind, what is the point in proceeding with these taxation measures at this time, because quite obviously the price of oil, gas and minerals depends on what takes place at the meetings in April? I should like the minister at least to comment on this situation. I know he cannot be specific, but he said that the differential between domestic and world prices should not be too great, or that the difference needs to be narrowed. It would be interesting to find out what the government feels the price difference should be in order to make sure that the oil and gas industry is healthy and can provide Canadians with a reasonably secured supply.
With the realization that the number of rigs drilling for conventional oil in Alberta has been reduced, it seems important that this resource taxation field be straightened out. By passing these two clauses it would seem that the government in effect is saying to the provinces that this is the federal government's stand, it cannot or will not back off, and if there are to be any changes the provinces will have to make them. Certainly the passage of these clauses can be construed as nothing else but a provocative and
February 24, 1975

antagonistic attitude toward the provinces. This attitude might not be so bad if we did not face the prospect that we are running behind in respect of cheap conventional oil.
Let us consider our balance of payments problems. We had a deficit on current account for 1974 of $2.5 billion, and it is estimated that we will have a deficit of $3 billion this year. Last year there was a surplus in petroleum, oil and natural gas of $1.6 billion. Oil imports are expected to bring to the petroleum trade alone a deficit of $2.3 billion in 1980, and $4.4 billion in 1984. Surely this will have a significant effect on the future of the country, and what the Prime Minister will decide with the provinces when he meets them will be of great importance, because overcoming oil deficits is an important and difficult problem for Canada to face. We would be less than prudent if we did not make sure that the oil industry had a reasonable return and there was reasonable activity to bring on new supplies.
With regard to minerals, again it seems here that these resources are not in as short a supply around the world as are gas and oil, and that the price of these products has decreased.
When it is stated that in 1975 the effective rate of tax in Ontario and Quebec will be around 60 per cent, added to the more than 100 per cent tax rate in western Canada, it becomes certain that investor confidence will be eroded, and the capital intensive mining industry will be even harder hit than it has been by inflation. The president of Noranda suggested that the cost of developing a new mine in February of 1975 is more than double what it was three years ago, and five times what it was ten years ago.
There is a question that I would like to put to the minister. I believe that in clause 7 there is a formula according to which royalties will be computed, based upon provincial gas company rates. I assume that this is specifically designed for the British Columbia Crown corporation. If the minister has not already done so, and to my knowledge he has not, I would like him to explain how this formula will be worked out and on what basis the fair price will be established. Will the price be based on the U.S. price at the border? 1 think this is a most important question, particularly if there is to be a proliferation of Crown corporations involved in oil and gas energy.

Mr. Chairman, I support the amendment put forward by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain that we delay the proclamation of clause 4 until after the meeting of the first ministers in April. I also want to say that I thought he made a brilliant speech today laying out the reasons why this is the position that the government should take.
It is very difficult to understand the comments which the Minister of Finance is reported to have made this evening, or why the government is taking such a rigid attitude with regard to this tax situation. It is really incredible, when all the opposition parties and nine of the provinces are very much opposed to this proposal, as well as practically all the industries involved, that the government insists on moving ahead.
Income Tax
We are not debating this evening a simple tax clause. We are coming to grips with an issue that is affecting everyone in this country. One can find no support for the government's position. It is arguing its case alone, and one finds it difficult to know what its case is, because it is not as if the federal treasury badly needed money at this time. It does not. It has been a long time since it has been in such a liquid position.
Surely the government must understand, and the minister must know what a fragile thing maintaining confederation, operating a government, and operating a country like Canada is and how much it requires co-operation and not confrontation.
Ever since the so-called oil prices development in the Middle East, we have lived through a series of confrontations in this nation-confrontation between the provinces, and confrontation between industry and the provinces, and confrontation between industry and the federal government. Surely this is no way in which to run a country, and surely the minister must realize that the hon. member this afternoon gave a very logical and rational reason why this clause should not be proclaimed until the conference of the first ministers has been held, or why indeed it should never be proclaimed at all.
The government's action has created enormous uncertainty within industry, which has had an adverse effect on the production of our ressources, and will have a great effect on future production. And again one wonders, why the government takes such a position since its policy in the last three years has been to fight inflation by increasing supply. The minister will recall that the opening lines of most of his budget speeches have been that we will fight inflation in this country by increasing supply. If there has ever been a proposal which has done more negatively to affect the supply of important resources in our nation than the proposal before us now, I do not know what it has been. Industry wants certainty. People in industry want to know that they will be able to make a fair rate of return on invested capital in order to be able to progress. It is abundantly clear that while the resources are here in Canada, the fact of the matter is that the capital, the know how, the knowledge to develop those resources and to get the supply that we need in this country, are found throughout the world. If industry cannot earn a rate of return on the development of the resources in this country, of course it will invest that capital elsewhere. It will move to other places where the return, in its view, is more appropriate.
This evening we are trying to find an effective solution for taxation of natural resources. It is a problem that affects everybody in the world. If anybody is paying any attention to what we are doing in this country, it must really amuse them to see, at a time when everyone is trying to find a way to increase the supply of oil and petroleum, that here we are in a country of 20 million people, one hundredth of the whole population of the world, locked in combat between one province and the federal government because we are not capable of working out a mutually agreeable system for developing resources.
Surely the confrontation approach that the minister has taken is no answer to the serious situation in which we find ourselves. I hope the minister will spend some time,

February 24, 1975
Income Tax
when he answers questions explaining why he has been rejecting out of hand the "Hamilton proposal," if I may call it that. The shortages which we are going to experience in the future will not only be in oil and petroleum but also in capital which must be used more effectively. With the rate of inflation that is being experienced everywhere in the world, the amount of capital that will be available for investment opportunities will be greatly decreased and the amount needed will increase.
One of the most challenging things we have to do is to find a way to use capital much more efficiently. All projections for the development which is going to take place in Canada during the course of the next quarter of a century suggest that we must make more effective use of capital. All the projects we are talking about are capital intensive; for example, the James Bay project, the Mackenzie River Pipeline project, if it goes ahead, and all the development which is going to take place in the tar sands. We will not be able to raise the capital we will need to develop these projects as inflation continues, and the government is going to have to participate in greater degree. The time will come when we must find a way to use capital much more efficiently and intelligently, not only in Canada but all over the world.
It is going to be an impossibility to undertake the sort of resource development we are talking about if it is intended to finance it in precisely the same way it was financed in the past. One can say there is going to be abundant capital available from the Middle East. That may be true. There have been large transfers of resources to the Middle East from the western industrialized countries, but surely we are not prepared to depend on financing from the Middle East in order to get our projects under way.
How can we use capital more efficiently? That seems to be almost as significant a problem for the minister as the entire conflict between the provinces. The real question is whether we can get these developments under way by turning capital around in a much more efficient and effective way. The proposal put forward by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain strikes me as providing one answer. What is being proposed is a simple matter of the government foregoing its tax revenue and the equity holders foregoing their rate of return during a period of time in which the proceeds from the investment are used to retire debt.
Briefly the net result of applying this proposal is that the debt is wiped out early in the life of a project. No matter how the arithmetic is applied, the net result for both industry and government is that they are infinitely better off because all the front end costs are disposed of. A large debt structure unfortunately absorbs a unique proportion of the output from any particular project, and it would be much better if this revenue were used as a rate of return for the equity investment, much better used as a source of tax revenues for the government of Canada in the interests of the people of Canada, than to service debt.
It is quite true that there is nothing more difficult to bring into effect than a new idea, particularly in the area of finance. It is interesting that the proposal of my colleague has now picked up independently developed sup-

port. I do not suggest it is coming from the same source, but it was referred to this afternoon. The British government is now looking at a proposal not altogether different which is outlined in The Economist of, I think, February 14. All round the world people are searching for a way to make more effective use of capital and to achieve a more rapid turnover.
I would like to know what is wrong, when a proposal is put forward of this dimension and significance and which is so important because we are going to be so short of capital, with taking the time to examine the proposal, to put it to the provinces and to industry for consideration. Why not postpone the proclamation of Clause 4 so that the federal government, the provinces and the industry may study the proposal?
I do not know what the government really wants, but unless it really wants to see this nation moving into a situation where the private enterprise system is not able to finance any of the major resource projects we have before us, it must find some new way of financing these particular projects. Is it really the aim of the government to make sure that practically all the major proposals in the future are going to have to be financed partially or entirely by government? If they are, we are going to be moving toward a type of economy which I do not think the people really want. We must explore new methods.
I cannot over emphasize to the minister and his advisers that this issue is not important only to Canada, it is not important only to the resource industry, it is not important only to the provinces, but it is really important all over the western industrialized world. Surely if there is a country where we could make an effort to make a breakthrough on this particular problem, it should be Canada. What is the need? What is the rush? Why is it important that we have an immediate solution?
I find it quite inexcusable to dismiss out of hand, without any real care or study or presentation to a single province, a serious proposition put forward by the opposition in this parliament. It seems incredible that the government should take that attitude. I have to agree with the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain that it is almost as if agreement has already been made that there will be a new budget which will satisfy some of the people involved in the current confrontation, but agreement certainly has not been made to help the hundreds of small Canadian companies suffering so much under this situation.
The proposal put forward by my colleague this afternoon seems emphatically logical, emphatically forthright and would get around the dilemma with which we are faced at the present time of confrontation that is bound to increase without solving any particular problem. The government may win this confrontation, but it really will win nothing in the long run because it is not dealing with the basic issues. I find it almost inexcusable that the government would not take under consideration the proposal made by my hon. friend this afternoon.
The proposal was made actually on January 30 in this House. It has not been discussed with the provinces or with other groups, and I would urge that the minister reconsider remarks he has made in the past and the remarks he made today that the government will insist on

pushing forward with this clause of the bill in face of the fact that the provinces, the opposition and most industries are opposed to it, in face of the fact that it can bring only difficulties to the fabric of confederation at the present time, in face of the fact that it is running counter to the policy of the government of trying to increase supply, in face of the fact that it will not do anything to solve the fundamental problem we will face, and are facing, of how to use capital most efficiently, and in face of the fact that a serious proposal of an alternative approach to financing has been put forward with the request that it be considered by the provinces and industry. What can the government lose by waiting and by accepting the proposition put forth today? It would seem to make good sense for the government to accept this proposition today.
Why go ahead and bring about confrontation which will not do anything for the country except great harm? When it comes time for the Minister to reply I hope that he will not dismiss the proposal put forward by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain out of hand but will give it serious consideration.
There is no advantage in the government doing what it has planned to do, and there is a tremendous advantage to the country by it accepting this amendment, and I hope it will do so.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I want to say that I was going to speak in this debate anyway-the fact that the government House leader came and sat beside me should not be construed as encouragement to speak.
I want to support the amendment, Mr. Chairman. I am going to take another view of it, however. The grounds advanced by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain have been harrowed and cultivated and there has been a little fertilizer from the government side so I am going to approach the question from a different direction.
Before doing so, however, I want to congratulate the government whips. There are members here on the government side from the province of Quebec, which has the traditional position of defending the constitution, and the fact that the government whips have been able to keep them quiet is a tribute to the way they operate. I am certain, Mr. Chairman, that if a number of members from Quebec had their way they would oppose the way in which the government, through this particular clause, has been trampling on the constitution. I think this is a real tragedy, Mr. Chairman, and my remarks will therefore be along those lines.
What is proposed by this clause and the related clause is looked upon by the Minister of Finance as part of the numbers game that he and his officials play with this question of the percentages of tax, and the refusal to accept the royalties of the provincial governments with regard to petroleum products or minerals as being a deductible item. The question of how to divide up the pelt of the skinned taxpayer has been a continuing battle between federal and provincial bureaucrats for many years. Ever since the Rowell-Sirois commission reported
Income Tax
and the government of Canada started to intervene-in many cases with the support of the provinces-this game has been going on. I do not suppose it will ever be concluded.
As I have said before, I think the government has gone a little too far. We may be now looking at the fall and decline of the federal system. Surely a federal system, particularly one which is to be successful and is to survive, must march in tune and in sympathy with regional and provincial aspirations-geographic, economic, racial, religious, and, of course, linguistic. For eight or ten years the present government has pursued a vigorous policy tied to the fact that linguistic differences must be maintained. It is far less accommodating, however, when it comes to other things.
Natural resources are not something over which the federal government has jurisdiction, or the provincial government has jurisdiction. The natural resources belong to the provinces, to the people of the provinces.
If one examines the confederation debate, or the debate which took place in 1930 when resources were returned to the western provinces, one will find that it was made abundantly clear at that time that those resources were to be the property-the royalties were to be the property of the people of the provinces.
In the course of that debate the late Mackenzie King was asked if royalties were going to belong to the people of the provinces, and the answer was yes. We are not dealing merely with the federal government invading a matter with respect to which the provinces have jurisdiction, Madam Chairman-this is property which the people of the provinces own. Now we find the federal government intervening and attempting to take something which does not belong to it. If someone had come to me with that story when I was practising law I would have said that the federal government had engaged in the act of theft- straight theft, and conversion of property belonging to someone else.
Now I must ask if we want the federal system to be continued in Canada because I think that is the problem we face. By a series of fortuitous circumstances, a bit of luck and some skill, over a hundred years ago we put together a document called the British North America Act. We have added to this from time to time, and it has preserved this country in pretty good shape in spite of the fact that we have been cursed with a Liberal government in 35 out of the last 40 years.
I suggest, Madam Chairman, that diversity and distinctiveness remain the basis of social progress-diversity between individuals and diversity between regions and provinces in a federal system. I know this is a doctrine which is an anathema to many of the social scientists who manage to burrow into the bureaucracy-I am going to read this and, because I think the committee should have the full benefit of it, I will repeat it. This business of diversity and individual distinction remains the basis of social progress. This is a doctrine which is an anathema to the social scientists who burrow into the internal processes of government and shortly set to work to produce the usual garbage-like litter of documents which is the centrepiece of all bureaucracy. In this way they manage to restrain the over-inquisitive natives when they get rest-

February 24, 1975
Income Tax
less, and permit the elite high priests of the government civil service to practise their trade and pursue their inclinations without hindrance.
I wish I could take out of the statutes of Canada the various amendments made to the Income Tax Act in the last three or four years. I see the hon. member for Edmonton Centre here. We all remember the occasion in the House some years ago when, with a superhuman effort, he managed to tear up that huge monument, the Income Tax Act. Even as the hon. member was doing that, the then minister of finance was given his reward. He became Chairman of the Canadian Transport Commission, and he has made as great, a shambles of that job as he did of the finance portfolio. This is what may happen to our present minister. I am sure the Prime Minister has something in mind for him. Even if the CTC is demolished, another agency will be established in its place, and a spot will be found in it for the Minister of Finance. I am sure the Prime Minister will be glad to see him there.
Now let's get back to the script.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
I say to the committee, without fear of successful contradiction, that few understand these voluminous income tax amendments. The distinguished gentleman sitting in proximity to the Minister of Finance, and I do not mean his seat mate, is one of the few in the chamber who understand this bill. I hear that many people who have tried to understand it have been on the psychiatrist's couch, and many are in institutions. I do not think anybody really understands this legislation, which is one of our difficulties.
I submit that passage of this clause will endanger the future of confederation. Even since the Rowell-Sirois Commission reported, federal governments have meddled increasingly with matters of provincial concern. This has been done through the Income Tax Act, and through general welfare and social security programs. It is somewhat strange that at the very time when provinces face tremendous financial burdens as a result of social security programs initiated by the federal government, the federal government is saying to them, "You people in the provinces will have to restrain your costs". The provinces must make expenditures at provincial levels because the federal government, which initiated these programs, has cast the burden on the provinces.
Passage of clause 4 would impose on the people of this country a pattern of rigid conformity which is not conducive to the future development of Canada and its people. I reject the principle of the unitary state. If we had wanted a unitary state, we could have provided for it 100 years ago; and I strongly resent the government's attempt to establish a unitary state by passing measures such as the one we are debating.
Speaking in defence of measures of the kind introduced in this bill and in the petroleum administration bill, the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources said that when the rights of the provinces, conflict with the rights of the people of Canada as a whole, the rights of the provinces must yield to the rights of the

people. Let us examine that statement which sounds good and reads well.
What are the ministers saying? When they speak of the people of Canada, they mean people concentrated in central Canada. Obviously since the people of Quebec and Ontario outnumber the rest, the representatives of those people, through their preponderance of numbers, will be able to introduce programs which will be acceptable in their provinces. True, you can do that; but you cannot do that and still have a valid federal system.
If there is to be a federal system, a system which will give effect to the rights of people living in the four corners of any province, we must heed the constitution. When that constitution says that natural resources belong to the people of a province, it does not lie within the competence of this or any other federal government, by using measures of this kind, to take away from the people of a province their rights of ownership and their right to deal with resources as they see fit.
The people who lead our provinces are reasonable and decent, and when they sit down at a federal-provincial conference they will work out programs and compromises which will be for the benefit of the people of Canada as a whole. This has always been the case, but it takes time. One can liken this process to some industrial disputes. The parties sit down at the bargaining table, then get up, but come back again. I have enough confidence in the people who lead the governments of this country, the governments of the provinces, to believe that compromises can be worked out.
But I say to this committee that this consensus cannot be achieved by the federal government's securing passage of legislation of this kind and then going to the bargaining table and saying, "We have this legislation on the statute books; you do what we tell you, or else!" That is not the way to secure understanding and compromise on which the resolution of these difficulties must be based. I suggest that there are people in the west, in the east, and in central Canada who say that if this is how the federal government operates, it is time we re-negotiated the conditions of confederation.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
I will not spell out how this could be done; it could be by means of weighted votes, changes in the other place-to which the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre might agree-or changes in this chamber, whereby the party system which has been inflicted on our parliamentary structure since confederation might be altered to provide for a greater measure of independence. This could be done in many ways. But I say to the members of this committee that demand for change will continue until it becomes a clamour which cannot be ignored.
Given these conditions, would the government not be sensible in saying, "We are prepared to defer proclamation of these objectionable and controversial clauses until we have sat down at the bargaining table and worked these matters out with the provinces, in the spirit of reasonable compromise which must be achieved if we are to survive and prosper as a country and if these difficulties are to be resolved"?
February 24, 1975

Confrontation is not good enough. I believe strongly in the adversary system, as a lawyer and member of this House. Under the adversary system we can examine an issue from all angles; the opposition can challenge the government and examine its programs from all angles. But when the adversary system is changed into a system of confrontation politics for political purposes, so that the dominant level of government can say to provincial governments, "We have the power; you do this or that, or else", I say that we have gone a long way down the road in deteriorating Confederation. If they, representing the majority of the people of Canada, decide that a certain thing should be done in the interest-in their opinion-of the nation, then apparently it does not matter a damn whether that action comes within federal jurisdiction or not; the government will take action regardless of the feelings of the provinces.
I have watched the minister as these speeches have been made. I feel the government is set in its position and I think it is tragic that its attitude cannot be changed. I can only urge the Prime Minister, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and the others who will be at that bargaining table in April to bear in mind what I have said. The hour is growing late. There is not much time in which to work out this problem.

Madam Chairman, I want to comment on the amendment and reiterate our support for it, and then move on to a series of questions which I hope the Minister of Finance will answer.
We are dealing with the resource sections of Bill C-49, especially the clauses which prevent royalties being deducted from revenue earned by corporations. This has the effect of inhibiting provinces in raising tax revenue as should be their natural right. It forces the provinces to back down on the attempt to gain through the imposition of royalties a fair return for their resources, many of which are non-renewable. I would like to mention for, the minister's edification, a fundamental concept which was stated clearly in the report of the Royal Commission on the Transfer of Natural Resources of Manitoba in 1929. This royal commission stated, and I quote:
At confederation it was decided to make natural resources the cornerstone of provincial sources of revenue. The provinces transferred to the federal government most of their other sources of revenue including, notably, the collection of customs duties, but they retained for themselves the use and control of Crown lands, mines, minerals and royalties as sources of income.
It seems to me that the government, through the budgets of May 6 and November 18, is making a determined attack on that fundamental right of the provinces. I think the amendment which was proposed to delay proclamation of these sections of the income tax bill relating to resources until the first ministers of the provinces and the federal government have been able to sit down and talk is quite justified. It is better we should talk about this vital issue rather than the Minister of Finance should in a high-handed way impose a tax scheme which is contrary to the very fundamental precepts of confederation.

Hear, hear!
Income Tax

The whole issue of resource taxation is a fundamental one. We have been dealing into the nondeductibility of provincial royalties, but there is one glaring omission from this income tax bill, a glaring omission on the minister's part to state clearly and precisely what the government's intentions are in terms of taxation policy toward the Syncrude project recently approved in principle by the government.
The minister has been telling us that the Syncrude deal and the oil company partners in Syncrude will be exempt from the provisions of this tax bill relating to resource taxation. But he is fudging the issue. He is not telling us precisely what is to be the tax regime governing the Syncrude project.
I have five very important questions which I should like to put to the minister; we in this party want clear and distinct answers before we dispose of this bill. We are prepared to sit here and debate it until we get clear answers from the minister.
The minister has been stating publicly that the Syncrude project will be exempt from the royalties nondeductibility provisions of the November federal budget. He is exempting this multi-million dollar Syncrude project yet he will not exempt other resource concerns in this country. If should be clear that Syncrude will be exempt from the royalties non-deductibility provisions which, of course, means it will enjoy an important tax concession as compared to other resource industries.
As my second question, I want to know if it is correct that Syncrude will also retain automatic depletion allowance of up to one-third of production profits instead of having to earn the depletion allowance and instead of being limited to a maximum of 25 per cent of production profits. That is a very important distinction, and we need a clear answer.
As my third question, will Syncrude be able to continue to claim 100 per cent write-off of development costs instead of being limited, as in this budget, to 30 per cent only for development write-offs? The Minister of Finance is saying that Syncrude will work under the 1973 tax regime; as I read it this means Syncrude will enjoy a 100 per cent write-off on development costs.
As my fourth question, under the provisions of the 1973 tax regime, as stated by the President of Imperial Oil and the President of Gulf Oil, is it correct that if Syncrude has insufficient profits to absorb all available tax write-offs, these write-offs can be passed back proportionately to the partners to be written off against their income from other sources of operation? As I read the bill, and as I understand the officials from the oil companies, they will be able to do this. This means a tremendous tax loophole exists for these companies. If Imperial Oil, for example, invests in Syncrude a sum of $300 million it can write off against its other operations taxable profits in an amount of $400 million odd dollars. It follows that the government will tax that much less of the profits of the oil companies from their other operations. They will be able to use Syncrude as a great tax deductible haven.
A further question I wish to ask: is it correct that the Syncrude consortium, because it is exempt from certain provisions of the November budget, will be assessed at a

February 24, 1975
Income Tax
lower federal tax rate of 48 per cent for 1974? Will the rate be 47 per cent in 1975 and 46 per cent in 1976, compared with the 50 per cent corporate tax rate which will be in effect for the other resource industries in this country?
Before the recent deal was made in Winnipeg that fateful Monday, the president of Imperial Oil was saying that if the government did not come through with equity financing he would be happy to revert to the tax scheme of 1973 for the oil company partners in Syncrude. Mr. Armstrong, according to the Globe and Mail for January 23, calculated that if the oil company partners in Syncrude could work under the 1973 tax regime, they would have a saving of upwards of $1 billion over a four and a half year period. If that is correct-and I have no reason to doubt the president of this oil company-it means that the Canadian people will end up financing 90 per cent of the Syncrude project.
We have been told by the government that the Canadian public, through the provincial and federal governments, is putting up 30 per cent of the costs, or $600 million. The government of Alberta has given the Syncrude partners a $200 million loan. That totals $800 million. If the tax regime of 1973 were applied to Syncrude then, in the words of the president of Imperial Oil, the Syncrude partners would get another $1 billion in tax concessions. In other words, the public would be putting up $1.8 billion, or 90 per cent of the cost of Syncrude, and would get in return only 30 per cent ownership. The companies would have 70 per cent ownership; the public, putting up 90 per cent of the financing, retains only 30 per cent ownership.
No wonder we call this the greatest sell-out in the history of Canada's resources. This is something that the minister has a duty to clarify for the benefit of the public of this country. He must let people know exactly what they have got themselves into. The public of this country has been duped; we have been sold out by this government and by the multinational corporations.
The other point the Minister of Finance and Minister of Energy do not like talking about too much is the rip-off in the Syncrude project in the form of a more than doubling of the price of oil coming out of the oil sands. This was another part of the agreement-that oil which is now being produced at $6.50 a barrel will be sold at the world price, which could range anywhere from $11 to $15 a barrel; that has been guaranteed the Syncrude partners. Yet they are going to be taxed at an even lower rate, according to the Minister of Finance, than any other resource company in this land.
Canadian consumers will not only pay outrageous prices for the privilege of using their own oil; they are, as I say, going to be financing this project through direct public funding and tax concessions which the government has given the Syncrude partners, for all of which they retain only 30 per cent of the ownership and decision making in this vital project. The Minister of Finance must come clean and tell the truth about this aspect of the Syncrude deal which he has so far failed to clarify in any speech made to date. We await with interest his defence, if he has one, of this outrageous sell-out.

Mr. Chairman, I do not want to preclude the minister from standing up and explaining this outrageous sell-out, or whatever was the term used at the end of the remarks of the hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie. Certainly I will defer to him in tonight's debate if he so chooses.
I feel somewhat intimidated in rising to my feet after the quality of the debate today. This afternoon the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain stated in very eloquent terms that there was a better way of accomplishing the goals that the minister, the government, and I think every member of the committee would like to achieve. Then the hon. member for Don Valley indicated there was really no need for the minister to proceed in the manner he chooses to proceed now. The hon. member for Peace River also pointed out that continuing to proceed in this way could be dangerous to the goals he indicated he would like to see Canada achieve, and which I think are shared by all members of the House.
Yet in face of all this reason, logic, rationale and superb debate, the minister sits Sphinx-like and unimpressed, indicating he still does not concur in the amendment to the clause proposed by my colleague for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain. That is regrettable. I am sure the hon. member for Peace River is entirely accurate when he says that continuing this stubbornness in face of reasoned and rational argument and positive alternatives that are clearly superior, is dangerous to the economic future of this country, as well as to confederation because of the tensions that are created.
Indeed, Madam Chairman, I am a little confused about the real purpose of this particular proposed section of the Income Tax Act providing for non-deductibility of royalties. I listened attentively, as I always do, to the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance during the budget debate when he outlined the reasons for this provision. These were along the lines that the greedy provinces had taken too much money, that there would not be enough money left for the oil companies to continue their exploration and development, hence this proposal. This convoluted reasoning I find a little difficult to understand since I fail to see how the oil companies, or anybody, will be able to maintain a viable operation in the face of taxation rates that exceed 100 per cent.
Perhaps the reason was more accurately stated this afternoon by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources who stated that the goal of this government was first, to achieve more revenue for the federal treasury, second, to allow some revenue to go to the provinces and third, if there was any left, to provide some revenue for the industry so it may maintain exploration and development programs to discover the oil and gas we need.
I suppose that is the nub of the problem and is an indication that security of oil supply in this country is the third priority of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, who should be concerned about Canada's longterm security of supply. Evidently he thinks it far more important to have revenue for the Turner-Trudeau empire, or should I say the Trudeau-Turner empire, so it might continue to grow at the rate of 28 per cent a year.
The whole story of how this particular aspect of this bill-the provision relating to non-deductibility of royalties-was introduced into the fiscal scheme in this country
February 24, 1975

is in itself a sad one. The method used in the budget of May 6 has been described accurately by my leader as a deceitful, dishonest approach.
At the January, 1974, meeting of the first ministers a uniform price for crude oil across Canada was agreed upon and there was no indication given at that time that the government contemplated the introduction of a measure such as this, but out of the blue on May 6 we found this proposal in the budget. Faced with the description of this by my leader, as a matter of deceit and dishonesty, the Prime Minister indignantly replied in a speech in the House of Commons, to be found in Hansard at page 1726:
Let me remind the House, for the record, of the earlier approach that we adopted at the end of January this year at an open conference televised for everyone to see, an approach which precisely was one of trying to get an agreement on the sharing of production profits. We have proposed a sharing.
The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources brought into that conference a document entitled "A Presentation to Provincial Premiers of Suggested Distribution at Alternate Prices of Revenues on Crude Oil Production". There are a number of suggestions here based on various wellhead prices for crude oil. There is a suggested wellhead price of $6 and the suggested distribution, and a wellhead price of $7 with another suggested distribution. If we average the $6 and the $7 we arrive at $6.50, which is the currently existing price. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, I am sure with the concurrence of the Minister of Finance, or certainly of Jack Austin, indicated a sharing and suggested that the oil producing provinces should receive 31 per cent of total revenue, including export taxes. The minister suggested that the federal government should receive, excluding the amount it uses to subsidize eastern consumers, 7.8 per cent of total revenue.
What does this budget do in the face of that suggested sharing? Prior to the budget the province of Alberta introduced a new royalty scheme which gave the province 23 per cent of the total revenue, in other words something like 8 per cent less than the federal government suggested. The province of Alberta under this scheme was to take 8 per cent less of the total petroleum dollar than the federal government suggested it should take at that January conference.
This budget, according to the Minister of Finance, would provide the federal treasury with 18 per cent of the petroleum dollar as opposed to the 8 per cent which was suggested at that time as being a reasonable figure. Faced with these facts, how could anybody describe the actions of this minister and this government in introducing these provisions as being anything but deceitful and dishonest? Certainly this is deceitful and dishonest, and totally out of keeping with the suggested distribution at that conference.
The Prime Minister had the gall to suggest that this document gave the provinces fair warning. That is an incredible suggestion. What is even more incredible is that the Prime Minister, the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources should raise their eyebrows and suggest that the provinces are just being greedy and selfish. They suggest they are just protecting the interests of the people of Canada against these greedy
Adjournment Debate
and selfish provinces which have not acted in good faith and will not discuss the matter with them. They say they would like to discuss this with the provinces, but the provinces cannot be counted on to sit down at a conference table and negotiate in good faith, but will go back and rob the kitty before they have a chance to get to it. The facts simply discount that suggestion. The facts will not substantiate that claim.
I should like to know whether the government has ever repudiated the sharing as suggested in this document that was tabled at the first ministers' conference. I suggest that one item on the agenda of the first ministers' conference on April 9 and 10 might be the re-discussion of this question of revenue sharing. If that is to be the case, the government will not want to be burdened with the restrictions in Clauses 4 and 7. It would serve the interests of the government, the country and everybody else, to have these restrictions set aside until after that conference.
As my colleague, the hon. member for Peace River, has pointed out, we have reached the point where Confederation itself is being threatened by this type of activity, with commitments made and borken, and unilateral moves by the federal government into areas which clearly lie within provincial jurisdiction, without so much as a by your leave or anything that could be considered as fair and just warning, and without even so much as a rational reason. As the hon. member for Don Valley has pointed out, it is not as though the federal government is strapped for cash. The Income Tax Act currently in existence is bringing in revenue almost as fast as the government can spend it, although nothing could bring in revenue that fast.
There a few other points I should like to make, but we have reached the hour of adjournment. May I call it ten o'clock?

subtopic: MANPOWER-OPPORTUNITIES FOR YOUTH PROGRAM-SUGGESTED INCREASE IN FUNDS TO COMBAT UNEMPLOYMENT IN ATLANTIC REGION
MANPOWER-OPPORTUNITIES FOR YOUTH PROGRAM-SUGGESTED INCREASE IN FUNDS TO COMBAT UNEMPLOYMENT IN ATLANTIC REGION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I was just about to say that my question on the late show tonight is important enough to have both the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras) and his parliamentary secretary here, but I notice that the minister scurried out as quickly as he could. I am glad the parliamentary secretary is still here.

February 24, 1975
Adjournment Debate
Mt. Turner (Ottawa-Carleton): We are listening to you, Jack.

subtopic: MANPOWER-OPPORTUNITIES FOR YOUTH PROGRAM-SUGGESTED INCREASE IN FUNDS TO COMBAT UNEMPLOYMENT IN ATLANTIC REGION
speechtext:
I am glad to see that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) is here.
Perhaps the parliamentary secretary might be able to give me a more positive answer than the one I received from the minister last week in the House when I requested the consideration of an extension of the funds allocated to the student summer employment program, and particularly the Opportunites for Youth Program. My reason for concern is that the steadily increasing unemployment rate in Canada, which will tend to worsen this summer if projected trends are correct, will cause intense hardship and discouragement to those who are affected most at that time. I refer to the age group between 14 and 24. None of us are proud of the fact that the national unemployment rate in this category is 11.8 per cent, seasonally adjusted, with the actual rate being 14.4 per cent.
Neither are we very proud of the over-all unemployment rate in the Atlantic region which, in January of this year, was 10.6 per cent, nor am I particularly proud of the over-all rate of unemployment in my province of Newfoundland, which in January was 16.1 per cent.
What concerns me in particular, Madam Speaker, is the fact that the number of persons between the ages of 14 and 24 in Newfoundland is well over 100,000, most of them in secondary schools or at university. Also, many of them must find jobs this summer to enable them to return to their studies.
As of January 1975, some 31,000 of our citizens are unemployed. This summer this number will multiply due to the many more thousands from the group I mentioned who will be seeking employment.
Certainly the same or similar figures hold true on a comparative basis right across the Atlantic region, and all across Canada in the slow growth areas.
The present OFY, funded at some $27.5 million, is expected to employ some 20,000 students. It is obvious that that amount of money and the projected number of jobs will not even scratch the surface of the problem. Even if we add the other programs, such as job exploration for school drop-outs, providing 550 jobs at $300,000; student community services providing 2,100 jobs at $5.7 million; youth hostels providing 550 jobs at $1.3 million; cadet training for 2,350 young people, and the portion of the 3,200 in the age category between 17 and 24 who will train with the militia; the 392 students who will be employed under community assistance; the 9,300 students who will be employed in the public service; and the many other programs such as drug research, street agencies, parks Canada, native summer employment, tourist surveys, improvement agriculture, many thousands of young people in this age category will be unemployed.
So we have programs which have proven successful in the main, and we have those that were wasteful and useless. What is needed is better control by experienced officials who will not only monitor the projects but create more employment. Even though it is hoped that the Canadian business community will employ thousands of

students this summer, I plead with the minister, through his parliamentary secretary, to try to impress upon his cabinet colleagues the necessity of increasing the funds for the students summer employment program, even though I was pleased to hear that the matter was under review.
This will allow more of our young people to follow the criteria laid down which will be of benefit to participants. The program will involve our youth, will allow them to use their initiative, not only to benefit the community but to relieve the pressures on them to finance their education, and provide them with the opportunities which they deserve. Most important, it will provide the many more jobs that are required for the youth of our country.

He and I share the northern peninsula of Newfoundland; we share the many communities which find themselves in a similar situation, and we share a concern for the young people in that area. We both know that the people in rural Canada will probably have less opportunity to take advantage of many of the programs offered than will young people in urban Canada.
While I share that concern, I think it is important to put on record what is being done. The hon. member of course has indicated many of the programs that will be in existence this summer in addition to the OFY program. He has mentioned that the total budget of the Students Summer Employment and Activities Program is $67 million, to be divided among 12 different federal departments, including the Department of Manpower and Immigration, the Department of the Secretary of State, and the Department of National Defence.

The Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) says it is a little early to see the bite of the budget. We will have to see what effect the budgetary measures taken earlier will have on the situation.
The hon. member has mentioned the cadet reserve training programs of the Department of National Defence, the student community services of the Department of the Secretary of State and the student employment offered by the Public Service Commission. These are going to offer summer employment to 37,000 young people. Of that 37,000 jobs, 20,000 will be created by Opportunities for Youth. There is a program, a comprehensive program, a widespread program with many different options for unemployed people in Canada, and in fact, unemployed people in the Atlantic area.
I would like to put on the record that under the 1974 OFY program 12.3 per cent of the budget was allocated to the Atlantic provinces. This year the amount is 20.7 per cent, a substantial increase to the Atlantic area. I may say

subtopic: TRANSPORT-INCREASING CANADA'S SHARE OF MARITIME TRAFFIC UNDER UNITED NATIONS ACCORD-GOVERNMENT POSITION
TRANSPORT-INCREASING CANADA'S SHARE OF MARITIME TRAFFIC UNDER UNITED NATIONS ACCORD-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my rising tonight is made possible by Mr. Henry Brown and flows from a series of questions I placed upon the order paper directed to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) on October 31, 1974, and again on November 4. These questions referred to the proposed code of ethics for the liner conference agreed upon by 72 of the member nations at Geneva in April, 1974. The principle purpose of this agreement, for the edification of the hon. gentlemen here, is to seek to express to the international shipping concerns the growing lack of ease felt in the world exporting and importing communities as to the level of service rendered and the extent to which this service reflects the national interests of those nations concerned.
It would seek to guarantee for the exporting or importing country an amount such as 40 per cent of the trade each way, with some 20 per cent left open for third parties. This proposal has a long way to go before it is ratified by sufficient member states to have the force of law on the seas, but is a step and a warning to the world that all is not well in the exporting and importing countries which have up until now relied so heavily upon international and foreign shipping concerns.
Canada, probably predictably, took no position. We have no fleet. We have, according to Howard Darling, not even an identifiable ministry responsible for maritime shipping policy.

subtopic: TRANSPORT-INCREASING CANADA'S SHARE OF MARITIME TRAFFIC UNDER UNITED NATIONS ACCORD-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Shame!

subtopic: TRANSPORT-INCREASING CANADA'S SHARE OF MARITIME TRAFFIC UNDER UNITED NATIONS ACCORD-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
We depend for 99 per cent or more of our export and import trade on foreign shipping. Put another way, Canada relies almost exclusively on the whims of the foreign shipping cartels, and these cartels, according to Howard Darling, are increasingly becoming owned or directed by the foreign governments through whose subsidies alone much of the world's fleets survive.
Canada's foreign trade is simply too vital to be left up to the interests of foreign powers. It is, in a word, under attack from increasing bilateralism, increasing foreign national ownership and financial participation, increasing specialization and increasing nationalism.
Our defences are weak, almost pathetically so. There is no responsible ministry, no responsible minister. Is it
Adjournment Debate
External Affairs? Is it Industry, Trade and Commerce? Is it the Department of Transport? No one seems to know, and I suggest no one in government seems to care.
One per cent of our trade is carried today in Canadian bottoms. The UNCTAD proposal would give Canada an immediate option to insist on upwards of 40 per cent. What does this mean? Again no one knows.
Standing on the order paper in my name are the following questions:
No. 1130: Has the government established any interdepartmental groups to examine the impact upon Canadian shipbuilding, ship repair and merchant seamen and officers of the possible ratification by Canada...
I am referring here to this agreement.
No. 1131: How many ships would be required to accomodate the movements (a) out of Canadian ports to foreign destinations; (b) into Canadian ports from foreign destinations of 40 per cent of the present liner conference rated cargo?
No. 1132: How many merchant seamen would be required to accomodate the staffing of the number of ships required ...
This would be related to the answer to question No. 1131.
No. 1133: How many (a) general cargo (including passenger cargo); (b) container type vessels were employed in the liner conference rated international inbound or outbound seaborne shipping to serve Canadian ports within the most recent 12 month period?
All of these questions have been on the order paper of the House of Commons for almost three months with not a trace of an answer to one of them. This is a disgrace, born of neglect.
I put down a motion for the production of papers. The government said that the convention was hypothetical and therefore Canada had done no study of it. But what then is to guide the decision with respect to ratification that Canada must take for itself? There is no answer.
I want to know what Canada is going to do. I suggest that the present stonewalling is a result of callous, foolish, bungling neglect-a neglect born of ignorance and fostered by a naive trust in foreign shipping concerns. This is not good enough. We must end the somnolence and sleepwalking that this minister and this government satisfy themselves with and act now to ratify a code of ethics.
I seek information tonight. On November 6 I wrote the Canadian Transport Commission seeking the size of the Canadian fleet. I have never received a written answer to this day, although I had a phone call which said that they did not know. They did not know, Madam Speaker, the size of Canada's fleet.
I wrote to Statistics Canada for some informations as to the impact this agreement would have on our fleets. They did not know, but for what they could provide they wanted me to pay $1,000. One thousand dollars for irrelevant material! Sadder still, the Dominion Marine Association never even acknowledged my inquiries.
I want to know how much money Canada loses in foreign exchange for shipping charges to foreign fleets. It has been estimated at over $1V4 billion each year-each year we have no fleet in Canada. Canada's history under successive Liberal administrations has been one of lost opportunities. I hope tonight we can start the long trail to

February 24, 1975
Adjournment Debate
a safe, predictable, profitable and constructive national flag fleet for Canada's international trade.

speakeroldname: Mr. Joseph-Philippe Guay (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Regional Economic Expansion):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion; Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: TRANSPORT-INCREASING CANADA'S SHARE OF MARITIME TRAFFIC UNDER UNITED NATIONS ACCORD-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I will answer solely the question put by the hon member. It is unfortunate that time does not permit me to answer all the comments he made this evening which were not included in his notice.
Even though the United Nations convention on a code of conduct for liner conferences concluded in Geneva on April 7, 1974, and a majority of countries voted in preference to accept the code, it is by no means certain that the code will ever be ratified by the necessary countries so that it can be enforced. As the member is probably aware, the code would become effective with the accession of 24 states with at least 25 per cent of world registered cargo tonnage.
I think it would be useful to point out the main reasons why Canada abstained. The approved code requires compulsory cargo sharing which would effectively remove competition in setting rates. The code provides for the establishment of a new structure for compulsory arbitration. The Canadian position was that this arbitration should be established within the existing United Nations structure. The code, however, provides for an elaborate new structure with the prospect of elaborate new costs which would have to be provided by the trading nations.
At the present time Canada is considering certain factors which will determinate whether or not Canada accedes to the code. I think it should be pointed out that only two countries, Iran and the Philippines, have signed. Another factor that Canada must consider is the attitude of her main trading partners. Thirdly, we must look into the compatibility of this code with other Canadian international agreements. Bilateralism and the 40-40-20 formula, to which the hon. member referred, may diminish the role of cross-trading and increase costs of intercontinental transportation. And last, but not the least important, we must look very carefully at the effect on Canadian domestic interests.
I believe the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) is on record as being inclined to support the idea of a Canadian merchant fleet. The circumstances which dictated Canada's abandoning its merchant marine fleet after the Second World War have changed greatly. The convention promotes national shipping lines, but the definition embraces even foreign ships under charter. Hence, accession to the convention would not in itself imply any commitment to develop a merchant marine.

subtopic: AIR TRANSPORT-DEFECT IN PRATT AND WHITNEY JET ENGINE-COMPLIANCE OF CANADIAN AIRLINES WITH MODIFICATION
AIR TRANSPORT-DEFECT IN PRATT AND WHITNEY JET ENGINE-COMPLIANCE OF CANADIAN AIRLINES WITH MODIFICATION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the topic I am speaking on tonight is one that concerns directly or indirectly a great number of Canadians. I refer to the subject of safety on our domestic airlines. This is a subject I have been investigating for some time.
I received confirmation from the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) that a Pratt and Whitney engine modification I had inquired about was to be performed on Canadian airline planes. I was gratified by this, but I am very concerned about some other problems in this field. In 1974 we saw a sharp rise in the number of fatalities on commercial flights abroad. In the United States more than twice the number of passengers and crew lost their lives in 1974, as compared with 1973, the number of deaths per 100 million passenger miles rising to .256 from .122.
I should like to ask the Minister of Transport a number of questions, for the purpose of ensuring that this rising fatality rate does not spill over into Canada's air industry. We have been fortunate so far, but a number of recent occurrences have given rise to a growing belief that the ministry of transport is not doing its job as far as air safety is concerned. One example was the revelation last year that dangerous air cargo was often being transported while improperly packaged or labelled, and with the air and ground crews being unaware of its contents.
The Ministry of Transport has also apparently failed to monitor certain problems with some air systems on domestic airlines. I have in my possession an Air Canada maintenance document that states that flight 526 out of Quebec City on March 26, 1974, depressurized, and that 40 per cent of the oxygen masks failed to supply oxygen. The company management has subsequently claimed that all oxygen systems have operated "within design tolerances". They have admitted, however, that the Douglas Company held a meeting in October, 1974, with a number of airlines on the subject of the DC-9 pressurization and oxygen systems, which are termed much "more critical" than those of other aircraft. As a result, Air Canada carried out 22 modifications on these systems with which, two months earlier, they had claimed there was "no problem". These discrepancies in information demand investigation.
Last Monday evening, Winnipeg International Airport was closed for three hours. Yet during the period the airport was closed an L-1011 belonging to Air Canada was given clearance to land-the airport management stated that the aircraft had an engine out, making it an emergency situation. Simultaneously, Air Canada stated there was no problem with the plane. Even if other sections of the Department of Transport are in a mess, the particular facet of the operation we are considering involves a regulatory body which is responsible for thousands of people's lives every day where mistakes can be tragic and fatal.
This morning's Montreal Gazette carried a front page story headed "Profits go First Class as Airlines put Safety Second." It states:
Safety regulations are being sidestepped routinely on most commercial flights in Canada including Air Canada and CP Air as airline officials and federal authorities turn a blind eye.
The well researched article goes on to quote a number of airline employees as saying that regulations concerning the taking on board of baggage that will not fit under the seats and forbidding passengers to sit beside emergency exits are ignored as a matter of course. Pilots complain that passenger bridges are withdrawn before the pilot

February 24, 1975

gives the okay. All employees agree that the management of the airlines stress no delays and no ruffling of passengers' feathers long before they stress conforming with the law.
It is further reported in this and an accompanying article that employees have been reprimanded for delays caused by their concern for safety regulations and at least one purser, who is named in this article, has been asked to resign twice by his direct superiors because of a pet concern for safety.
When charges such as these, combined with the examples of ministry of transport negligence I have cited, appear on the front page of a respected Canadian newspaper, the government has no choice but to initiate an independent investigation into the enforcement of MOT regulations and the conduct of our domestic airlines in complying with those regulations.
I would also like to ask the Minister of Transport whether or not his department has plans to require a device known as the ground proximity warning system to be installed on all Canadian airlines. This device senses an aircraft's rate of altitude change and height above the ground, signalling when evasive action is necessary to avoid a collision. It costs between $10,000 and $15,000 per aircraft, and is to be made mandatory by the FAA in December.
The subject matter of my speech could be discussed when Bill C-226 comes before the Standing Committee on Transport. Bill C-226 is an act to provide for the constitution of a federal transport commission of inquiry which would impartially investigate traffic accidents, safety standards and regulations. The United States is setting up such a safety board. It is no longer proper for the ministry of transport to be investigating itself.
I would like to say, in conclusion, that it has been brought to my attention today that the Ministry of Transport fire trucks at Vancouver Airport do not have ladders long enough to reach the second deck-

subtopic: AIR TRANSPORT-DEFECT IN PRATT AND WHITNEY JET ENGINE-COMPLIANCE OF CANADIAN AIRLINES WITH MODIFICATION
speechtext:
The hon.
Adjournment Debate
member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. McKenzie) has chosen to deal with a number of matters other than the one involving the Pratt and Whitney aircraft engine of which he gave notice. In any case, I believe the hon. member is to be lauded for his continued concern in the area of passenger safety.
As he is aware, aircraft and aircraft components such as engines are strictly monitored, and regulations concerning safety are strictly enforced. Indeed, I can say they are religiously adhered to by Canadian airlines. All Canadian air carriers have taken the appropriate action specified by the aircraft engine manufacturer, Pratt and Whitney. The United States Federal Aviation Administration is issuing an air worthiness directive on this subject which will require inspections of the shaft. Compliance with an air worthiness directive issued by the aeronautical authorities of the country of manufacture of an aircraft is a condition of a Canadian air worthiness certificate. It is not necessary for our ministry to duplicate such directives.
In view of the fact that the hon. member made reference to the Montreal Gazette, I should like to point out that many of the points made in the newspaper article are grossly exaggerated. As a matter of fact there is some evidence that the individuals selected for interview by the reporter, David Tafler, are not aware of MOT's increased activity and the several meetings that have taken place with the air lines during the last six months. I do not believe that the marketing personnel of the air carriers have the authority alleged by Tafler.
In regard to the suggestion that certain of these members have been speaking in an irresponsible manner, I have been in touch with the head office of the Canadian Air Line Pilots Association and they are equally surprised by the appearance of the article in the newspaper, and are attempting to ascertain who among their members have been speaking out in such an irresponsible manner. Probably more facts will emerge, but I am pleased that this point was brought out.
I would remind the hon. member that Air Canada has always considered safety of its passengers before any other consideration. I think the safety record of Air Canada speaks for itself; it has one of the best records in the world.
